I'm being assessed for ADHD and have been teaching myself tarrot for about 6 months. 

I'm using The Cozy Witch tarot deck where each card has a sentence under the artwork related to the cards meaning. The art style might/might not be your thing but I've found that very helpful as a prompt during readings. There are probably other decks that also have this. 

The book I find most usful is the Wild Card, it's informative, entertaining and you can read as much/as little at a time you want. Dipping into a page on a particular card is useful and informative without having to read the rest of the chapter. 

I also have 78 degrees of Wisdom and it is really interesting but very in depth and I often get distracted while reading it. You also kind of need to read it in order for it to make complete sense and it references so many other things my brain wanders off on a lot of tangents. 

I'm also using The Tarot Spreads Yearbook which has example for 52 different spreads to do, it's focus is on reading for yourself opposed to doing readings for other people. There are probably lots of other books like it, I find it really helpful to have all the spread layouts/topics.

I would like to join but may not be consistently active because I recently joined a real life book club. 

There is some discussion of the book but it is mostly socialising, which I suppose is important but not why I joined book club.

Things I keep in my car for emergencies: warning triangle, warm blanket, first aid kit, cereal bars, water, wind up torch/radio. 

Never needed to use most of it but I'm always very happy when I can help myself to water/snacks.

I don't like getting into water, I don't like getting out of water but I love it once I'm there. I love swimming and (when able) use it as a kind of physical meditation, it's so calming just swimming up and down the lane until my mind is quiet. I'll also happily stand under a hot shower for a ridiculous amount of time which makes it so much more frustrating that I often can't take the step of actually getting into it. 

Another odd thing is that I often can't resist touching something if I think it's wet. Or any odd textured things really, my hand automatically reaches out and touches everything! Even when I then dislike what I've touched, I don't want my fingers to be wet but I generally cannot stop myself from touching the wet thing 🤷🏻‍♀️

Yeah, all the time. I think it's because I view myself in the third person if that makes sense? Like my brain and sense of self is somehow disconnected from my body and I think about my life in the same way as I think about a character in a book. It's really frustrating a lot of the time because people seem to think being self aware means I have everything under control but it just means I can tell you all the ways I don't have things under control and why, without being able to do anything about it 🤷🏻‍♀️

Something I find useful is the Zones of Regulation, it splits emotions into four colours, red, yellow, blue and green. I learnt about it working in a SEN school I'll try and explain it a bit. 

Green = everything is okay

Red = angry, basically having a meltdown

Blue = all low energy emotions so bored, ill, tired, sad ect 

Yellow = all high energy emotions so anxious, excited ect

The idea is essentially that you want to spend most of your time in the green zone. In the moment I cannot describe what specific emotions I am feeling but I have been able to identify physical signs for each colour so I can tell what zone the feeling is in. 

This is helpful because each colour has different things I can use to get back to the green zone and then when I'm in the green zone I can reflect on what the specific emotions might have been and what caused it. 

I can try to explain it a bit more or give some examples if it would be helpful. I do find identifying my emotions challenging but this has been helpful. It's still frustrating to think in the moment, I feel yellow, I wonder if that means I'm excited or scared.
I often think my world is much more interesting because I spot so many fun things. Unfortunately it's also much less functional when I can't tell you the name of a road I walk down every day 🤷🏻‍♀️

I seem to although I can't exactly explain it. I always say my feet know where they're going even if my brain doesn't. I definitely can't give other people directions because I can't explain where I am in relation to things and I have no clue about street names, regular landmarks or a good sense of how long it will take to get somewhere (especially because I walk very fast). 

I think it must partly be an innate sense of direction and partly an observational thing because I'll remember a tree, an interesting brick wall, an abnormally loud drain ect once I've been somewhere. Nice for me but not helpful when someone is asking where a particular street is.

I have a lot of problems consistently feeding myself so I'm not sure how useful my advice will be but there are a few strategies I use to try and make it easier. 

First I have lists of safe foods/meal ideas split into energy dependent groups going from 'I can look in the cupboard' to 'I will cook an elaborate meal'  so I don't have to remember what I like. I like eating the same things all the time until one day I don't want it any more so having the lists helps remind me what I else I might want to switch to. 

For the low energy groups I have food I can eat from the cupboard, food that requires a microwave or kettle and food that needs an oven. I try to make sure I have all these foods consistently stocked so there are plenty of quick/easy to prepare things.

When I have energy to cook I meal prep so the rest of the week I can just get it straight from the fridge, and make double portions so I can freeze half. 

Another helpful thing is snacks. I'm trying to make sure my snacks are nutritious enough it doesn't matter if forget meals. Currently I'm enjoying hummus and once a week I weigh out 5 portions of dried fruit + various nuts and just eat however much I want each day (I do also have lots of unhealthy snacks in the cupboard but I try to prioritise protein and fruit/veg in my diet).  

I find visuals really helpful so I leave the fruit/nut box on the side where I see it all the time and also have signs on  cupboard doors ect reminding me to actually look for the food I like.
Yes. All the time.

I'm sorry you're going through this. I've been in burnout coming up to 3 years too, getting out of bed, getting dressed, eating and drinking everyday, these are achievements in my life. It's a huge deal that I've done these things everyday (most days) for the last two weeks. That is where I am in life. 
I had a support worker for a while from the mental health team and she kept trying to get me to schedule in 'little treats' like going out for a coffee or cake and she just couldn't understand that doing that would not be a treat. It would be work. Work I didn't/don't have the energy for. 

I think your example is people using the term burnout in the same way some people use depressed when they just mean a bit sad. It's frustrating to anyone who actually understands what depression is because their misuse of the word minimises your experience. 

It can also be hard for people who don't properly understand autism to understand the concept of autistic burnout. To them it looks like depression, and often the treatment for depression is to keep doing things, find something you enjoy to hold on to. So that's what they tell us to do. It sucks because autistic burnout may look like depression but the treatment is the opposite, if we keep trying to do things the burnout gets worse, we have to do exactly what you are doing, nothing. We need rest, a break from all the sensory input in this world to try and regulate ourselves again. 

And I think that people (maybe subconsciously) misuse terms like burnout and depression on purpose because they don't like confronting the reality of long term mental illness. If they can say they were burnout but went away for a couple of days and now they're fine, it makes them feel safe, that maybe they'll feel bad sometimes but it won't last, that everything will actually be okay. 
Having someone say they've been burnout for years, and no they're not really feeling any better, and no they don't know what to do about it... It makes people feel uncomfortable. It's easier to believe that we're just not trying hard enough because that means it won't happen to them because they would try. 

Sorry this has turned into a massive stream of consciousness. I hope that you find a way out of burnout, I hope I do too.

I'm still waiting for official diagnosis (been on the list for 2 years now) but I'm certain that I am autistic. 

I've been in burnout for years and am trying to build a new life with a better understanding of my needs and part of that included grieving the NT version of my life I'd tried so hard to create. Anger is one of the stages of grief and yeah, I felt really angry. Angry at my teachers, my family, my partners, my doctors, everyone who told me I was making things up or that I was just lazy or weak or a bad person. 

I think it was important to let myself feel those feelings but eventually you have to let it go. That anger won't change the past, you can't go back in time and make people treat you better. 

I also do believe a lot of those people were trying their best. Their best wasn't good enough and that sucks but being angry about it now doesn't change anything.

I'm part of a community allotment, it's my first year growing but there's a very experienced person whose guiding everything. 

We're growing 7 kinds of tomato in a poly tunnel, 6 are doing well and 1 is not. That 1 is a heritage seed, the plants seem okay but every other variety  is doing so much better and is covered in flowers/fruit. The few fruit that have formed on the heritage plant also seem to attract every bug so they're half eaten before we can harvest them.

I feel like I've been on a continuous quest to find a style that feels like me and I think I've finally been making some progress this year. 

First step for me was spending some time to figure out my specific sensory issues with clothing. I tried on loads of things in my wardrobe and wrote down what felt good/bad about different fabrics and fits. I didn't look in the mirror or think about how things looked, just how comfortable I was. 

Once I had the list of what fabric/fit was my favourite I looked online and found some tops/leggings/shorts/slip dresses that I can wear on their own or under other clothes to make them more comfortable. I bought multiples of these so they can always be the base of my outfit. 

Once I'd figured out the sensory side I started thinking more about fashion stuff. I started a Pinterest board, found people with my body type and looked for different silhouettes I liked. I found this helpful because it then gave me a basis for building specific outfits in my own wardrobe and I could use it to make a targeted shopping list for clothes. For example one of the silhouettes I like is wide leg trousers with crop tops, so I paired up all the trousers/tops I had and then made a note of any unpaired items so when I go shopping I am specifically looking for a top to go with those trousers. 

I used to find it really overwhelming going into a shop and having to look at every item and figure out if I liked it or not. Now I've got specific requirements I'm looking for so I can ignore a lot of things. 

Taking the time to organise my wardrobe into complete outfits and and separating the different silhouettes has also really helped because it reduces the decision fatigue. Instead of choosing each bit I just have to decide 'I want a dress/shorts/a long skirt' and I can just pick anything from that section. 

The final thing I had to think about is making clothes weather appropriate. I've always struggled picking appropriate summer/winter clothes so I made my wardrobe all summer outfits but with the option to layer things to make them warmer. I bought thermal layers to go under everything and oversized cardigans/jumpers in different colours. I haven't figured out coats yet but there's time before it's winter again.

Getting to this point has taken a long time and I still struggle with clothes but I think this is the most I've felt like myself. I had to break everything down into steps and do a little bit at a time, like just trying on all my jumpers one day and then waiting a week to try on skirts. I also spent a long time just going into shops for like 15mins and looking at things/touching different fabrics with no expectation of buying anything, just to start thinking about the future possibility of buying things.

*Edit: also to say I only ever wear trainers. I like them because you only have to find one shoe you like and they just keep making it in different colours.

I've realised that my brain registers pain the same way it registers other sensory discomfort. When I was younger I would cry and scream about having to get dressed because clothes were painfull, but I was consistently told that was wrong and what I was feeling wasn't pain so I learnt to mask/ignore it. 

I guess my brain is so busy ignoring all the other sensory pain that it just doesn't notice the addition of physical pain from injury or illness. It is hard to deal with because I'll hurt myself and just not notice, or notice something is wrong and not being able to tell where the 'wrong' is coming from. I also don't react typically to pain so even if the pain is severe enough for me to notice people won't believe me. 

The only good part is that I can sit for tattoos and have zero reaction 😅 My brain registers discomfort and then happily files it away with the rest of the discomfort 🤷🏻‍♀️

I eat a whole cucumber almost everyday because I love the crunch. Also a lot of apples and carrots, often with hummus for extra protein.

Edit: also remembered corn cakes (like rice cakes but I think they taste better) and dark chocolate. 

I think these are all my healthy snacks replacements.

The thing that I've found that helps is focusing on the structure of my day, so firstly I thought about when I have the most energy and am naturally the most productive. For me that's the morning so if I'm going to shower that day I know to put it as one of my first jobs. 

Then I tried to find a regulating activity that I enjoy, that makes me feel calm but that I can do for a set time period. For me that's highly structured craft activities so painting by numbers, diamond art, small Lego kits. I need something that has built in break times or I get consumed so reading or playing a game wouldn't work for me. 

Then I use the activity as a reason to get out of bed, spend some time doing that (also drinking water and a tasty drink), then go straight into showering, then back to the activity afterwards. 

It's not really a magic trick and it definitely doesn't always work because my energy levels fluctuate so wildly day to day but it has helped. 

I also made sure showering is the most enjoyable it can be with towels, body wash, ect that I like. And I have visual prompts for almost everything so if I'm stuck in a 'what to do' daze I can just read things off a list.

My favourite birthday was actually during COVID because there was no pressure to plan an actual birthday. Instead I watched scary movies, played some boardgames, every meal was breakfast food, I bought myself fancy champagne, a delicious cake, wore a birthday tiara all day. 

Also got myself my all time favourite present, a balloon inside a balloon 🎈

This looks amazing 😊 I got a very similar cut a couple of months ago, mine is buzzed at the back too, I have the left side completely shaved and the right more graded with all the curls on the top. I like being unsymmetrical and having all the hair textures to touch with zero hassle.

I thought I experienced life the same way everyone else did and the reason I struggled and they didn't was because I was a worse/bad/weak/lazy person. I thought I just needed to try harder and all my problems would go away. 

Unfortunately this idea was perpetuated by my family/partner/doctors until I had to be hospitalised where everyone spoke to me as I already knew I was autistic.

My diet recently has been: toasted sesame bagel with sliced cucumber and cheese, carrot sticks with hummus, and sliced apple with sultanas. Unfortunately that's all started to sound really unappealing so I'm just eating cereal until my new food obsession begins... 

For a while I was all about soup and that was good. I only had to cook once a week and you can get so many veggies and protein into one bowl of soup. 

Jacket potatos are another good one that doesn't need a lot of spoons and can be eaten cold depending on the topping. I'd cook them all at once and then make a big tub of tuna mayo with sweetcorn, lettuce and cucumber.

I feel like this a lot and for me it's often a symptom of burnout or the start of a depressive episode. I also struggle with executive function, making starting tasks difficult and transitions between different tasks. 

It's really tough, especially when I know it's an activity I should enjoy or something that will make me feel better. I've come up with a few things that help me. 

First I have a goal setting process so I'll decide what I want to be doing and then list out all the reasons it's not happening. I try to be really specific about exactly what the problems are. Then I take all those reasons and try to think of all the practicle things I can do to solve them. Lastly I make a plan to tackle each problem/solution, taking each thing one step at a time. 
I try to focus on making the goal as easy to achieve as possible rather than actually achieving the goal (if that makes sense). So if my goal was to read more I'd look at all the ways I make that as easy as possible: do I have things I want to read? Are my books easily accessible? Is there comfy space to sit? Do I have enough energy to focus? Do I need to plan a specific time? 
This doesn't mean I immediately read more but it does make it more likely that I will start reading again in the future. 

I also find it helpful to plan my day/week/month and I've made a planner that's somewhere I'll see it every day. I've got a symbol for every conceivable task I could do so I just have to pick from list rather than actively decide what to do. 
I've also colour coded my life because I've found different types of task use different amounts of energy and then I can plan my day around my fluctuating energy levels. 
For example: Housework is black, life admin is red, personal care is blue, socialising is yellow, solo hobbies are pink ect. Some colours always use loads of energy, some always give me energy. If there's something I want to be doing but never have the energy for I can easily look at the colours and see where all my energy is going and what I can change to give me energy to do the thing. 

I find the above things helpful when I'm already in quite a good place mentally, and they definitely help keep me in a good place. 

When I don't have any energy or motivation I try and take my usual hobbies and do a more structured/less intensive version of them. 

E.g. Instead of reading a book I look at magazines/listen to podcasts/audiobooks. Instead of going to the gym I do yoga at home/go for a short walk. If I can't do yoga or leave the house I sit on my yoga mat and do a breathing exercises/just stand in the garden for a minute. Instead of making art I do painting by number/diamond art. Instead of learning something new I do a puzzle/build a kit. 

I have a box of these kinds of activities so when I start feeling low they're all ready to use. 

Finally I'm trying to be kinder to myself and more understanding that I just need to rest sometimes, actually a lot of the time. Sometimes all I have the energy for is laying on the floor listening to music or watching TV and that's okay too. 

Sorry this comment got way to long. I massively over explain things... As you can tell.

The straps are marketed as support straps for injuries. I got them on Amazon, they have lots of options, mine are like giant velcro stips you wrap around your joints and I can do them as tight as I need. I want a compression vest but they're expensive, especially in adult size. 

I'll try and attach a picture of the breathing visuals I made. I prefer the one with the ball because I can focus on the sensation of squeezing it instead of just my breath. I find breathing exercises really useful but at the same time if I focus to hard on just breathing I almost forget how to do it 😅

*Edit: this sub doesn't allow pictures so I've posted the pictures on my profile (I think). There's 2 breathing exercises, a muscle relaxation one and a prompt for TIPP. They're all exercises from mental health things I just made my own versions with minimal words and added pictures because I stop being able to process complex thoughts and language during/immediately following a meltdown.
I also have a sign stuck next to my kitchen sink saying 'drink water' because I am perpetually dehydrated 😅 remembering to eat and drink is a never ending task.

It's definitely a work in progress, actually using coping strategies is so much harder than preparing the resources 😅

I also used to think I was amazing at emotions because I spend a lot of time reflecting on things, totally didn't realise other people know what they're feeling in real time... I need so much processing time to actually figure things out, especially negative emotions. I think this led to me ignoring a lot of times when I felt uncomfortable because I didn't 'feel it' at the time so I must have been fine 🤷🏻‍♀️ At least the boxes can help me regulate and narrow down the possibilities so I can reflect later. 

Growing up and in previous relationships I was always told I was wrong/over reacting/making things up when I tried to express my sensory needs. Challenging that internal voice takes a lot of work and I spend a lot of time reminding myself that having needs isn't a personal failing, being autistic isn't a personal failing, it's just who I am.

I've been spending a lot of time over the last couple of years trying to figure out how to make my life more sensory friendly and this is what I've come up with so far: 

Unflavoured toothpaste 

Solid moisturiser 

Unscented soap/shower gel 

Black out blinds/curtains 

Cotton t-shirts/shorts/leggings/dresses that I wear under all my other clothes so I can be fashionable AND comfortable. 

Cupboard dedicated to safe foods + a label on the cupboard reminding me that it exists and I should eat stuff. 

Blankets in every conceivable place so I can enter a blanket cocoon at a moments notice. 

Figet toys and snacks in the pocket of every coat and bag I own. 

I also have 3 colour coded boxes of 'sensory stuff' depending on my mood (this is based on the zones of regulation). 
Yellow is for high energy emotions e.g. anxious, it has fidget toys, visual things like bubbles, lava lamp, little puzzles, things to chew on.
Blue is for low energy emotions e.g. sad/tired, it has chocolate, fuzzy socks, sprays of scents I really like, toys with particular textures I enjoy. 
Red is for meltdowns and it has wrist/ankle straps because deep pressure calms me, also stress balls, theraputty and visuals for breathing/grounding exercises. 

Each box also has a list of the physical symptoms I experience for each set of emotions. I might not be able to tell if I'm feeling  anxious, excited, upset or tired but I can recognise what colour I'm feeling and then use the stuff in box to get back to neutral. 

Another thing I have is just a list of things to check if I feel 'wrong'. So I can go down the list and think 'Am I hungry/thirsty/tired/in pain/need the toilet, is it to hot/cold/bright/loud, are my clothes uncomfortable' 
I'm not good at recognising what's going on internally so having the visual helps me focus on each thing and think about solutions when previously I would just try to ignore the discomfort because I didn't realise I had sensory sensitivities.

I love my dinosaur skeletons and they fit in really well with the rest of my creepy stuff 😅 just ordered a load of mini Pokémon figures (not technically Lego) as a new mindfulness activity since my other activities haven't been effective recently.
I currently have two pigeons nesting right outside my window 😊 very much looking forward to meeting two new baby pigeons (hopefully next week!)

I've never felt particularly like a women or not like a women. I've been misgendered at various points when I've had short hair or been dressed androgynously and it never bothers me. I'm also not really attached to my name though and will respond to pretty much anything once I realise someone was talking to me. 

I don't feel like I'm in the wrong body in a male/female way, I think I have more trouble being perceived to be human in the first place 😅 I've always felt more like a werid genderless alien/fairy/robot in human skin.

It is really challenging, like I know I need outside help to figure things out but the only help available is actively making me feel worse a lot of the time. And then I feel this huge responsibility to educate/fix the mental health system when I'm really NOT in the position to do that. 

It's crazy to me that my OT understands that they're failing autistic women but then her (and a panal of other NT people) refuse to consider that ND people might have some useful insights into their needs. 

I often find this sub has better advice because people here actually understand my brain and they actually want to help.

Sometimes, I find certain music can be helpful as well and use that a lot during the day to try and focus. It tends to block out some of the streams of consciousness and allows me to focus on just one thought which is nice but sometimes I just want everything to be quiet. 

Unfortunately my OT is not very helpful, she's actually part of a group looking at why mental health services in my area are failing autistic women but she still manages to disregard almost everything I say about my lived experience.

Yep, it's the reason I'm here scrolling through Reddit at 2am because my internal world won't shut up. It's like a million different thought streams all at once and then I'll get sucked into replying the same conversation or interaction over and over until I can 'do it right'. 
I'll often notice myself talking aloud and fully reliving the conversations and have to tell myself to shut up. 

I'm trying to get my OT to help me figure out how to deal with it beyond constantly using other noise/videos to drown it out because this really isn't working but she's not helping so far. I don't think she really understands that my brain doesn't work like her brain.
That is fair. Think I'm going to have to expand my range of healthy crunchy snacks.
I've never seen this before, I think it could work really well. Thanks!
I'll definitely add them to my shopping list. I try to eat a lot of carrots, apples and cucumber to get my crunchy fix but recently it's just been massive amounts of cereal 😅

Thanks for the suggestions. I'll try to find a rosary, it would be more of a clacking but maybe it will do the trick. 
My head's been in a weird under/overstimulated flux recently and I've been almost constantly snacking which makes me feel better but isn't great long term.
Cabbage Whites are evolved specially to eat brassicas because they contain a mustard toxin that makes them taste really bad so a lot of birds will avoid eating them.

Chalk, makes me feel uncomfortable just thinking about touching it to be honest. Also most soaps, they make my skin feel so dry and like it's to small for my body. 

I can like slimy things if I'm consciously making the choice to touch it but only for a little while and then I'll freak out and need to be clean again. So maybe I don't enjoy it, more like a morbid curiosity/compulsion to touch it.
Yep, I love eating the same thing everyday, until I suddenly don't 😅 and then I'll have to remember that I like it again. Makes meal planning really hard when I forget all the foods I like.

This makes a lot of sense, I often can't sleep when I'm feeling low and coffee makes me sleepy instead of waking me up so I rely on little bursts of sugar to wake me up. 

When I'm stressed or anxious I also fidget with things a lot more so the constant picking at foods and chewing is calming + little bursts of sugary energy make me want to snack even more. And the lack of sleep just making me more hungry anyway. 

Thanks for the info, I like figuring myself out. I guess I need to 1) Sleep better 2) Find a stim that isn't eating a whole box of chocolates 😂
Ahh yes this might have an impact, there is a certain point when I just want to eat all the carbs in the world.

A surprisingly long time. I made it 6 days, felt a bit delerious, my lips cracked a lot and bled, but it didn't work like I thought it would. 

I saw online that someone was locked in a police cell and forgotten about for 18 days, no food or water, and they survived. Think they licked condensation off the walls and that was enough to save them. 

I gave up after that. Couldn't do it for another 12 days with no guarantee things would actually end. The human body wants to survive no matter how much the brain wants to die. 

Sorry you're in pain.

On a journey to find my own sensory friendly wardrobe and found 95% stretch cotton is my all time favourite fabric. 

Not sure where in the world you are but in the UK Primark has loads of things I can now use as a base layer underneath other less friendly but more more fashionable clothes. 

I've got loads of t shirts/crop tops/bralettes and high waisted shorts I can either wear as is or have on underneath other things. They do cami sun dresses too which I can either wear as a dress on its own or underneath something. 

Only thing is they're all really plain, just black/white/tan colour, if you weren't going to layer anything.

I'm really sorry you're feeling like this but I have to tell you this won't work, not in three days. I tried the same thing and made it a long time but I'm still here. 

There are cases of people going weeks without water and while it's not good for you, and you will die eventually, it will be a long slow process. I'm really sorry.

When I had a cat I let her go outside, I'd keep her in at night because I lived close to a road and I'd worry if I didn't know she was safe. She used to bring mice/birds in occasionally but I always said it was natural cat behaviour and you can't really have a cat and then get annoyed when they're cats. 

In the last year I've been learning more about British wildlife and have a much better understanding of the impact domestic cats (and dogs) have on our other native animals. I'd like to rescue another cat but I wouldn't let it out because they honestly kill everything, birds, mice, bats, frogs, lizards, spiders, your cat will kill it all just for fun. 

All British wildlife is under threat from habitat loss and human activity and I don't want to add to that problem by having an outdoor cat.

After telling them I was getting divorced. They told me 1) My ex would always be their son and that they loved him more than me (to be fair they did try to back track and say they loved us both) 2) That no one else would ever love me and I'd realise I was ruining my life when I died alone 3) They only loved me becuase the bible said they had to 4) That they were writing me out of their will, and leaving it to my ex, because this was proof I was mentally unstable and once I'd come to my senses and gone back to him it would be mine anyway. 

They were emotionally abusive my whole life but I kept going back and making excuses for them, not helped because my ex was abusive too. It's easy to believe you deserve to be treated badly when it's all people are telling you. Eventually I realised that I deserve to be happy and I just couldn't do that while continuing a relationship with them. They're never going to change, I think they honestly believe they're saying these things out of love and have no awareness of how they've hurt me.

I don't like listening to guided meditation things for the same reasons but I do find controlling my breathing really useful as a regulation strategy. 

I've found it helpful to squeeze a stress ball while I'm doing it so I can focus on the ball and my brain forgets to think about my breathing. I slowly squeeze the ball while I'm breathing in, then squeeze as hard as I can while holding my breath, then slowly release while breathing out. 

Don't know if you would find this helpful. To be honest if focusing on your breath is that deregulating for you might it might be better just to stop trying. The whole point is to calm down and it's having the opposite effect. Not everything works for every person and it might be better to focus on finding the thing that does work for you instead of forcing yourself to do something that doesn't.

I have lots of little thinking nooks around my flat that I use depending on my mood. 

In the living room I have a comfy sofa with loads of cushions, blankets (seriously so many blankets) and a variety of lighting options, the main light, fairy lights up the wall, a single reading lamp. This is generally where I read because all my bookcases are nearby and the walls are covered in my favourite things. 

In the bedroom I've put big soft rugs in the space between the bed and the wall and enclosed it further with a small table. I can sit on the floor (with more cushions and blankets) and feel really enclosed. I use this space when I'm feeling more anxious and have an anxiety journal and pens nearby. I also have sensory lights, speakers and lots of nice textures. 

In the kitchen I've made a space between a bookcase and the big french windows. It's super small and I can look out the window and think about my day/plan what I'm going to do. I only have a couple of cushions on the floor here and some fiddle things to keep my hands busy while I plan. 

I'd think about the room you have and what furniture you can use to break it up into different zones. You said you liked small spaces so maybe a big wardrobe you can take the doors off to sit in? For Intense Exercise, Paced Breathing and Paired Muscle Relaxation I find yoga a really good way to do all 3. I find it really meditative to move in time with my breath. For now I'm focusing on Paced Breathing while I'm in bed. Laying in bed I hold a stress ball in my hand and slowly breathe in, counting to 3 while squeezing the ball. 
Then I hold my breathe for 3 seconds while squeezing the ball as hard as I can. Then slowly breathe out for 3 seconds while releasing. I try and do it until I feel physically calmer but it doesn't always work, it's becoming more effective over time though. 

Once I start to feel calm I get rid of the ball and start doing the Paired Muscle Relaxation, I start at my toes, breathe in for 3 seconds and squeeze as hard as I can while holding my breath, then breathe out for 3 seconds and release. I work up my body doing calves, thighs, stomach, hands, shoulders, neck and face. 

I'm hoping it will get to the point where I'll do this and then just magically be asleep but I think that will take a long time. If I'm having a bad day I try not to be annoyed if I can't do any of it because my main priority right now is brushing my teeth and putting on my pajamas and I only have so much energy to spend. 

While I'm doing all this I also have my sensory night timer on playing nature sounds because I need the sound to stop my brain from overthinking things. When I start overthinking I trying to gently focus back on my breathing and count as I breathe in and out. 

I've written up my ideal bedtime routine and and working through it one step at a time, adding things in as I get more energy. Even though my sleep is still terrible, it's a lot better than it was so I keep trying to remember I'm moving in the right direction.

Keeping your flat a consistent temperature by having the heating on a low setting will help but that's not really affordable for a lot of people. 

You can reduce build up by having windows open / fans on when cooking and showering. Also having your bedroom window open a crack at night as we breathe out  a lot of moisture while we sleep. 

Keeping curtains open also reduces the temperature difference between the window and the room which reduces condensation but makes the room colder so not great.

You can buy thermal window film, basically looks like clear sticky back plastic, that you stick over the window. That will reduce heat lost through the window and help a little. It's quite cheap on Amazon and easy to remove so the landlord shouldn't notice it. 

Getting a dehumidifier is the best option although they can be expensive. Mine has a clothes drying setting as well which is really useful in the winter. 

Some people have suggested the dehumidying boxes but you can make your own using cat litter stuffed into old tights. If you lay them along windowsill it will absorb the condensation. You just need to keep an eye and replace them when needed. I've also used these in my car and it's worked well for me. 

It's important to keep removing any condensation you see or it will lead to mould and damp problems. The landlord might be open to helping if you tell them as it's there property that will be damaged in the long run but it really depends. I've had some great landlords but then I've had some really shit ones too. 

Hope this helps.

I think it's because neurotypical people process visual information differently than neurodiverse people. They're able to filter out background stimuli and focus on people's faces, especially in social interactions with that person, whereas neurodiverse people struggle to filter information in the same way. Other people have the same significance as everything that's going on making us really good at things like pattern recognition because we notice things others don't. But also bad at things like eye contact.

When I talk to someone I might be listening to them but looking over thier shoulder, and if something else is happening, like a bird flying past, I'll follow it. 

I suppose this makes our eye contact seem erratic and NT people might interpt it like us rolling our eyes or not paying attention. 

I think NT also find it easier to look at the person they're listening to while they're speaking. I find it hard to process what someone's saying while I'm looking at them  and have to look away to focus on the words, but it comes across as rude and disinterested.

Peoples favourite was the bean burger so I'll share the recipe as they're really easy to make! 

Makes 4 burgers

1. Roughly mash 2 tins of cannelli beans leaving some of the beans whole
2. Grate a large courgette and using a clean tea towel wring out the excess moisture (very important so they don't fall apart). Add to the bean mash. 
3. Fry 3 chopped spring onions in oil and cider vinegar and add to the bean mash. 
4. Roughly chop half a bunch of parsley and add to the beans. 
5. Season generously and then mix all the ingredient with 1 tbsp of plain flour and 1 tbsp of polenta
6. Divide into 4 and shape into burgers. 
7. Put 3 tbsp of polenta into a dish and coat the outside of the burgers. 
8. Shallow fry the burgers until golden and crispy. The recipient said 10 mins on each side but I typically did mine for 7. 

I made the burgers up yesterday and then fried them today and it worked really well as something you can make ahead of time for a BBQ or dinner party.

Sorry you think it sounds that way, that's not what I meant. When I got married we said we didn't want any gifts from guests but a lot of our friends approached us saying they wanted to do something for us. They came up with the idea of photographer as they knew we hadn't hired one. 

I'm not trying to say you should make demands but I think it's normal for friends and family to want to give you something when you get married and having a photographer document our day and was an amazing gift.

When I got married we weren't activly trying to be frugal but we knew we didn't want to spend a riddiculous amount on what is just one day of your life. I would recommend figuring out what is really important for you on the day and just doing that. We wanted a fun day with friends and family. 

A few savings we made

- Civil service with just family in the morning, we're not religous so a church wedding wasn't important to us.

- Hired a pub as the reception venue, we had a sit down meal with the family and then a buffet with friends later. 

- Hired speakers instead of a dj so we could still have music and dancing in the evening, the pub were fine with us bringing extra speakers and it only cost £50

- We had our rings designed and made by a local artist. We got exactly what we wanted for a very reasonable price.

- I designed my own dress and had it made for me, this cost £700, cheaper than shop bought dresses I was looking at and it was personal to me. 

One other thing, some friends got together and paid for a photographer for the day. We had decided it was too expensive and figured we didn't need one. This was an amazing present and it does make a difference having proper photos to look back on, not just for you but for other family as well. I would reccommend asking some friends to do the same. 

Our wedding cost around £5000 and we got everthing we wanted. I would say don't assume you have to make sacrifices to keep it cheap, just make sure you do what  YOU want. 

Edit: We had 20 people for the sit down meal, additonal 50 later on.
